verses.zh: 你当为以色列的王作起哀歌，
verses.en: “And you, sing[NOTE:1] a lament for the princes of Israel,

verses.zh: 说：你的母亲是甚么呢？是个母狮子，蹲伏在狮子中间，在少壮狮子中养育小狮子。
verses.en: and say: “‘What a lioness was your mother among the lions!She lay among young lions;[NOTE:1] she reared her cubs.
notes: Lions probably refer to Judahite royalty and/or nobility. The lioness appears to symbolize the Davidic dynasty, though some see the referent as Hamutal, the wife of Josiah and mother of Jehoahaz and Zedekiah. The background for Judah being compared to lions seems to be Gen 49:9.

verses.zh: 在它小狮子中养大一个，成了少壮狮子，学会抓食而吃人。
verses.en: She reared one of her cubs; he became a young lion.He learned to tear prey; he devoured people.[NOTE:1]

verses.zh: 列国听见了就把它捉在他们的坑中，用钩子拉到埃及地去。
verses.en: The nations heard about him; he was trapped in their pit.They brought him with hooks to the land of Egypt.[NOTE:1]
notes: The description applies to King Jehoahaz (2 Kgs 23:31-34; Jer 22:10-12).

verses.zh: 母狮见自己等候失了指望，就从它小狮子中又将一个养为少壮狮子。
verses.en: “‘When she realized that she waited in vain, her hope was lost. She took another of her cubs[NOTE:1] and made him a young lion.
notes: The identity of this second lion is unclear; the referent is probably Jehoiakim or Zedekiah. If the lioness is Hamutal, then Zedekiah is the lion described here.

verses.zh: 它在众狮子中走来走去，成了少壮狮子，学会抓食而吃人。
verses.en: He walked about among the lions; he became a young lion.He learned to tear prey; he devoured people.

verses.zh: 它知道列国的宫殿，又使他们的城邑变为荒场；因它咆哮的声音，遍地和其中所有的就都荒废。
verses.en: He broke down[NOTE:1] their strongholds[NOTE:2] and devastated their cities.The land and everything in it was frightened at the sound of his roaring.
notes: The Hebrew text reads “knew” but is apparently the result of a ד/ר (dalet/resh) confusion. For a defense of the emendation, see L. C. Allen, Ezekiel (WBC), 1:284. However, Allen retains the reading “widows” as the object of the verb, which he understands in the sense of “do harm to,” and translates the line: “He did harm to women by making them widows” (p. 282). The line also appears to be lacking a beat for the meter of the poem.

The Hebrew text reads “widows” instead of “strongholds,” apparently due to a confusion of ר (resh) and ל (lamed). L. C. Allen (Ezekiel [WBC], 1:284) favors the traditional text, understanding “widows” in the sense of “women made widows.” D. I. Block, (Ezekiel [NICOT], 1:602) also defends the Hebrew text, arguing that the image is that of a dominant male lion who takes over the pride and by copulating with the females lays claim to his predecessor’s “widows.”

verses.zh: 于是四围邦国各省的人来攻击它，将网撒在它身上，捉在他们的坑中。
verses.en: The nations—the surrounding regions—attacked him.They threw their net over him; he was caught in their pit.

verses.zh: 他们用钩子钩住它，将它放在笼中，带到巴比伦王那里，将他放入坚固之所，使他的声音在以色列山上不再听见。
verses.en: They put him in a collar with hooks;[NOTE:1] they brought him to the king of Babylon;they brought him to prison[NOTE:2] so that his voice would not be heard any longer on the mountains of Israel.
notes: Or “They put him in a neck stock with hooks.” The noun סּוּגַר (sugar), translated “collar,” occurs only here in the Bible. L. C. Allen and D. I. Block point out a Babylonian cognate that refers to a device for transporting prisoners of war that held them by their necks (D. I. Block, Ezekiel [NICOT], 1:597, n. 35; L. C. Allen, Ezekiel [WBC], 1:284). Based on the Hebrew root, the traditional rendering had been “cage” (cf. ASV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV).

The term in the MT occurs only here and in Eccl 9:12, where it refers to a net for catching fish. The LXX translates this as “prison,” which assumes a confusion of dalet and resh took place in the MT.

verses.zh: 你的母亲先前如葡萄树，极其茂盛（原文是在你血中），栽于水旁。因为水多，就多结果子，满生枝子；
verses.en: “‘Your mother was like a vine in your vineyard,[NOTE:1] planted by water.It was fruitful and full of branches because it was well-watered.
notes: The Hebrew text reads “in your blood,” but most emend to “in your vineyard,” assuming a ב/כ (beth/kaph) confusion. See L. C. Allen, Ezekiel (WBC), 1:284. Another attractive emendation assumes a faulty word division and yields the reading “like a vine full of tendrils, which/because…”; see D. I. Block, Ezekiel (NICOT), 1:607, n. 68.

verses.zh: 生出坚固的枝干，可作掌权者的杖。这枝干高举在茂密的枝中，而且它生长高大，枝子繁多，远远可见。
verses.en: Its boughs were strong, fit[NOTE:1] for rulers’ scepters; it reached up into the clouds.It stood out because of its height and its many branches.[NOTE:2]
notes: The word “fit” does not occur in the Hebrew text.
Heb “and it was seen by its height and by the abundance of its branches.”

verses.zh: 但这葡萄树因忿怒被拔出摔在地上；东风吹干其上的果子，坚固的枝干折断枯干，被火烧毁了；
verses.en: But it was plucked up in anger; it was thrown down to the ground.The east wind[NOTE:1] dried up its fruit;its strong branches broke off and withered—a fire consumed them.
notes: The east wind symbolizes the Babylonians.

verses.zh: 如今栽于旷野干旱无水之地。
verses.en: Now it is planted in the wilderness,in a dry and thirsty land.[NOTE:1]
notes: This metaphor depicts the Babylonian exile of the Davidic dynasty.

verses.zh: 火也从它枝干中发出，烧灭果子，以致没有坚固的枝干可做掌权者的杖。这是哀歌，也必用以作哀歌。
verses.en: A fire has gone out from its branch; it has consumed its shoot and its fruit.[NOTE:1] No strong branch was left in it, nor a scepter to rule.’ “This is a lament song, and has become a lament song.”
notes: The verse uses language similar to that in Judg 9:20.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the four modern translations above.
Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: EZEKIEL 19:1-14

1"As for you, take up a lamentation for the princes of Israel 2and say,

'What was your mother?

3'When she brought up one of her cubs,

Because of the sound of his roaring.

On every side from their provinces,

And brought him to the king of Babylon;

11And it had strong branches fit for scepters of rulers,

And its height was raised above the clouds

So that it was seen in its height with the mass of its

branches.

12But it was plucked up in fury;

It was cast down to the ground;

And the east wind dried up its fruit.

Its strong branch was torn off

So that it withered;

The fire consumed it.

13And now it is planted in the wilderness,

In a dry and thirsty land.

14And fire has gone out from its branch;

It has consumed its shoots and fruit,

So that there is not in it a strong branch,

A scepter to rule.

This is a lamentation, and has become a lamentation.'"

19:1-9 These two verses describe the exile of two Judean kings.

- Jehoahaz, taken to Egypt by Necco II

- Jehoiachin, taken to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar II

19:1 "take up" The VERB (BDB 669, KB 724, Qal IMPERATIVE) literally means
"to lift" or "to carry." Here it is used in an idiom for "speak loudly" or "make heard."

It is surprising that this chapter does not start with "the word of the Lord came to me
saying" (cf. Ezek. 1:3; 6:1; 7:1; 11:14; 12:1,8,17,21,26; 13:1; 14:2,12; 15:1; 16:1; 17:1; 18:1; 20:2,45; 21:1,8,18; 22:1; etc.). Does this
imply that chapters 18 and 19 form a literary unit? I think not since chapter 19 has two poetic lamentations (i.e. three beats per line and
then two beats per line of poetry).

▣ "lamentation" This term (BDB 884) refers to a specific type of funeral song (cf. Ezek. 2:10; 19:1,14; 26:17; 27:2,32;
28:12; 32:2,16). It becomes a literary marker for a new topic (genre, cf. Isa. 14:3-21; Amos 5:1-3). In prophetic literature there are several
standard oracle forms.

- promise oracle

- court terminology

- funeral dirge

A good brief discussion of funeral rites in Israel can be seen in Roland DeVaux's Ancient Israel, vol. 1, pp. 57-61.

▣ "the princes of Israel" This title ("prince," BDB 672) is used in Ezekiel to refer to several groups.

- King Zedekiah, Ezek. 7:27; 12:10,12; 21:25

- leaders of Judah, Ezek. 21:12; 22:6; 45:8,9

- future Davidic kings, Ezek. 34:24; 37:25; 44:3; 45:7,16,17,22; 46:2,4,8,10,12,16,17,18; 48:21,22

- foreign kings, Ezek. 26:16; 27:21; 30:13; 32:29; 38:2,3; 39:1,18

The term implies members of a royal family. Here, because it is PLURAL,
it refers to the king and others of his extended family in places of leadership.

19:2-9 This section of the lamentation refers to the kings of Judah, from the death of Josiah until the fall of Jerusalem (586 B.C.).

- Jehoahaz (Shallum, cf. Jer. 22:11), 2 Kgs. 23:31-33; 2 Chr. 36:1-4, who was Josiah's son and successor,
but exiled by Pharaoh Neco II after three months and replaced by

- Jehoiakim (Eliakim), 2 Kgs. 23:34-24:7, who was also a son of Josiah. He reigned eleven years and died. He was replaced by

- Jehoiachin (Jeconiah, Coniah), 2 Kgs. 24:8-17; 2 Chr. 36:9-10, who reigned three months and was exiled to Babylon (cf. Ezek. 19:9, 597
B.C.) by Nebuchadnezzar II and replaced with

- Zedekiah, 2 Kgs. 24:18-20, who was placed on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar II. He rebelled and was captured, blinded, and exiled to Babylon.

Special Topic: Kings of the Divided Monarchy

▣ "lions" See Special Topic: Lions in the OT

19:2 "your mother" This refers to

- Judah (cf. Ezek. 19:10) producing a line of Davidic kings (cf. Gen. 49:9; Num. 23:24; Rev. 5:5). This ceased with Zedekiah's exile.
In a sense (i.e. tribe of Judah but not family of Jesse), Zerubbabel (Sheshbazzar, Ezra 1:8) continued the Davidic line (cf. Haggai 2:23; Zechariah 4).

- The wife of King Josiah producing two sons (i.e. Jehoahaz Zedekiah)

19:10-14 These verses change the imagery describing Judah's royal family not as a lion pride but a huge,
tall grapevine. They also change time frames back to the beginnings of a unified kingdom (i.e.
Saul, David, Solomon). The vine is described as

- Positive

- planted by waters, Ezek. 19:10 (cf. Ps. 1:3)

- fruitful, Ezek. 19:10

- full of strong branches, Ezek. 19:10-11

- tall above the clouds, Ezek. 19:11

- Negative

- plucked up in fury, Ezek. 19:12

- cast down to the ground, Ezek. 19:12

- east wind dried up its fruit, Ezek. 19:12

- strong branch torn off, Ezek. 19:12

- planted in a wilderness, Ezek. 19:13

- planted in a dry land, Ezek. 19:13

- burned, Ezek. 19:14

The royal family was decimated (similar to chapter 17).

The lion imagery for Judah may refer to Jacob's prophecies about his children (esp.
Judah, cf. Gen. 49:9). Balaam also used this imagery to describe Israel (cf. Num. 23:24; 24:9).

19:12 "the east wind" This term (BDB 924 CONSTRUCT BDB 870) is used in
Ezekiel many times (over fifty), but most often in chapters 40-48 simply as "the east." It denotes

- the direction of the rising sun

- imagery for destruction (i.e. desert wind), often with the added theological connotation of
being sent by YHWH to accomplish His purposes.

- Gen. 41:6,23,27 (negative)

- Exod. 10:13; 14:21; Isa. 11:15 (positive)

- Wisdom Literature, Job 27:21; 38:24; Ps. 48:7; 78:26 (representative sample)

- Isa. 27:8

- Jer. 18:17

- Ezek. 17:10; 19:12; 27:26

- Hosea 13:15

- Jonah 4:8

- Hab. 1:9

- used as imagery to describe YHWH ‒ Exod. 15:8-10

The hot desert wind (Arabic, "sirocco" wind), like the rain, is at YHWH's disposal!
Wind (BDB 924, ruah) is often associated with YHWH's power (i.e. Spirit) in the OT.

Special Topic: Breath, Wind, Spirit

Special Topic: Spirit in the Bible

19:13 This is imagery for the Neo-Babylon exile of most of the population of Judah. There were several deportations
(i.e. 605, 597, 586, 582 B.C.). This specific context is referring to the exile of the legitimate Davidic king (Jehoiachin).

19:14 Fire is YHWH's instrument of judgment (cf. Ezek. 15:4; 20:47-48). There will be no Davidic king after the exiled Zedekiah.
Even Zerubbabel (Sheshbazzar, Ezra 1:8) was only a prince of the line, not a direct son. The direct son of 2 Samuel 7 will be the Messiah.
